You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out}$ between 1.8V and 3.6V, ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$, startup $\le 0.4\text{s}$, settled $\le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (at nominal $I_p=50\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}$).
    *   The previous attempt (`SSHI_FullBridge`) failed miserably ($V_{avg}$ below 1.8V for most cases).
    *   Looking at the previous circuit: It had a full-bridge rectifier *and* an inductor/switch.
    *   The combination in `SSHI_FullBridge` was: Full bridge (D1-D4) + an inductor (L1) in series with a switch (S1) connected to the piezo terminals.
    *   Wait, the previous circuit `SSHI_FullBridge` as described:
        *   D1: pzp -> out
        *   D2: pzn -> out
        *   D3: 0 -> pzp
        *   D4: 0 -> pzn
        *   L1: pzp -> n1
        *   S1: n1 -> pzn
        *   This is a parallel combination: a Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) and a resonant inverter (L1, S1).
        *   The resonant inverter (S1, L1) is essentially shorting the piezo across its capacitance $C_p$ to "flip" the charge. But the FBR is always there. This is not a standard SSHI. Standard SSHI uses a switch to flip the voltage and *then* rectifies.

    *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ is quite low. The FBR has two diode drops (approx $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$).
    *   The FBR reference results: S1 (2.24V, OK), S2 (1.76V, FAIL), S4 (1.51V, FAIL).
    *   The FBR is almost there for S1, but fails on S2 and S4 due to low voltage.
    *   The goal is to improve efficiency.

    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) typically uses an inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement (which are the zero-crossings of the current).
    *   Standard SSHI: At the voltage peak, the switch closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, $V_{Cp}$ is flipped, then the charge is transferred to the storage cap via a diode.
    *   Let's try a simpler, more effective SSHI topology:
        1.  Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        2.  Inductor $L$ in series with switch $S$ across the piezo.
        3.  A diode $D$ from the piezo to the output cap.
        4.  But since the piezo is AC, we need to handle both polarities or use a half-wave/full-wave approach.

    *   Wait, the $V_{oc}$ is low (3.2V). A full bridge might be too lossy. But a half-bridge or a charge pump?
    *   Let's try the "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI) or a basic SSHI.
    *   A basic SSHI structure:
        -   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        -   Resonant path: `pzp` -> `L1` -> `S1` -> `pzn` (controlled by SYNC).
        -   Rectification:
            -   Standard SSHI uses a diode from `pzp` to `out` and the ground reference `pzn` to `0`.
            -   Since `pzn` is not necessarily ground (it's a floating source), we can't just ground it.
            -   Actually, the piezo is modeled as a current source between `pzp` and `pzn`.

    *   Let's rethink: $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$. FBR is $\sim 2.2\text{V}$.
    *   The problem is the voltage drop. If we use a synchronous rectifier (switches instead of diodes), we could save $0.5\text{V}$. However, we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.

    *   Let's look at the FBR failure again:
        S2: $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$ (Need 1.8V)
        S4: $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$ (Need 1.8V)
    *   The FBR is very close! The main issue is $V_{out\_min}$ and $V_{out\_max}$ (S3 is too high).
    *   Wait, for S3, FBR gives $V_{avg} = 5.68\text{V}$, which exceeds $V_{max} = 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   So we need:
        1.  A way to boost the voltage slightly for S2 and S4.
        2.  A way to clamp the voltage for S3.
        3.  A way to reduce ripple.

    *   A Zener diode (DZ33) can clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V. This solves the $V_{max}$ issue.
    *   To boost the voltage for S2 and S4, an SSHI-like inversion is good.

    *   The "SSHI_FullBridge" attempted previously was a parallel combo of FBR and resonant inductor. The problem was that the resonant inductor was likely dissipating energy or interfering with the rectifier without effectively boosting the voltage.

    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" with a clamp:
        -   `pzp` -> `L1` -> `S1` -> `pzn` (SYNC edges=both, flips $V_{Cp}$)
        -   `pzp` -> `D1` -> `out` (DSCH)
        -   `pzn` -> `D2` -> `0` (Wait, `pzn` is the other side of the piezo. A diode from `pzn` to `0` would conduct when `pzn` is negative. This is part of a full-bridge).

    *   Let's try this topology:
        -   L1, S1 in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` to `pzn`). This flips the voltage $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks.
        -   A full-bridge rectifier (D1-D4) to the storage capacitor.
        -   $C_{out}$ for ripple.
        -   $D_{zener}$ for $V_{max}$.

        Wait, the previous `SSHI_FullBridge` was exactly this! Why did it fail?
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out (Wait, this is not a full bridge. A full bridge is: `pzp`->`out`, `pzn`->`out`, `0`->`pzp`, `0`->`pzn`).
        Looking at the components of Design 1 again:
        `D1: pzp -> out`
        `D2: pzn -> out`
        `D3: 0 -> pzp`
        `D4: 0 -> pzn`
        This *is* a full-bridge.
        `Dz: 0 -> out` (DZ33, Zener)
        `C1: out -> 0`
        `L1: pzp -> n1`
        `S1: n1 -> pzn` (ctrl=G1)
        `G1: SYNC`

        Why did it only get $0.9\text{V}$?
        The L-S combination was `pzp` -> `L1` -> `S1` -> `pzn`. This is in parallel with the piezo.
        If the SYNC `ton` is too long or the timing is wrong, it will just short out the piezo.
        The `ton` was $34.1\mu\text{s}$. For $L=4.7\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $\tau = \pi\sqrt{L C_p} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{4.7\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.08\text{e-5} \approx 34\mu\text{s}$.
        The `ton` is correct for inversion.

        Wait, look at the `vavg` for `SSHI_FullBridge`: $0.933\text{V}$.
        But the FBR (without L-S) got $2.24\text{V}$!
        Adding the L-S resonant circuit *decreased* the output voltage? That's impossible if it's just in parallel.
        UNLESS the switch is closed at the wrong time or for too long, which essentially shorts the piezo and dumps the energy into the inductor's resistance (though $R_{series}$ is small).
        Actually, in a standard SSHI, you *cannot* have the rectifier and the flip-switch in parallel like that without a way to isolate them, or the rectifier will just dump the charge into the inductor.
        In a standard SSHI, the flip happens, and then the diode allows the charge to flow to the load. If the diode is always there, the inductor might just be oscillating the charge back and forth through the diode.

    *   To implement SSHI properly:
        1.  The inductor-switch should flip the voltage.
        2.  The rectifier should move the charge to $C_{out}$.

        Wait, the most simple and effective "boosted" rectifier is the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or a simple SSHI.
        Let's try a different approach. The FBR is almost perfect except for S2, S4, and S3's $V_{max}$.
        S2 and S4 are the "weak" cases.
        If we can't get SSHI to work easily, can we just improve the FBR?
        No, the FBR is a passive limit. We need to boost the voltage.

    *   Let's try a simpler SSHI:
        -   Instead of a full bridge, use a half-bridge with a capacitor.
        -   Or, use a charge pump.

        Actually, let's try the "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI) again but more carefully.
        In P-SSHI, the inductor is in parallel with the piezo, and it's switched at the peaks. The energy is then harvested by a rectifier.
        If the previous one failed, maybe the `ton` or `phase` was slightly off, or the `L` value was not optimal for the tuner.
        Wait, the tuner *should* have found the best `L` and `ton`.
        If it failed that badly ($0.9\text{V}$ vs $2.2\text{V}$), the topology itself might be causing a problem.
        If the switch $S_1$ is closed, the piezo voltage $V_p$ is shorted through $L_1$. If the diodes are also connected, the charge might be flowing in a loop: $C_p \to L_1 \to S_1 \to C_p$, and the diodes just add loss.
        But the diodes are in series with $C_{out}$. Once $V_{out}$ is $1.8\text{V}$, the diodes only conduct if $V_p > V_{out} + 0.25\text{V}$.

        Wait! I see the problem. The `S1` switch is `pzp` -> `L1` -> `S1` -> `pzn`.
        This is a loop. If $S_1$ is closed, $C_p$ and $L_1$ resonate.
        The current in the loop is $I = V_p / \sqrt{L/C_p}$.
        This current will flow through the loop. It *doesn't* necessarily go to the output.
        To get the energy to the output, we need the rectifier.
        But the rectifier is *also* connected to `pzp` and `pzn`.
        The current from the $L-C_p$ resonance will also flow through the diodes.
        $V_{pzp}$ will oscillate. When $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_d$, it charges $C_{out}$. When $V_{pzp} < V_{out} - V_d$, it's blocked.
        This is exactly how SSHI is supposed to work.
        Why did it result in $0.9\text{V}$?
        Maybe the `C1` (storage cap) was too small? $22\mu\text{F}$ is usually plenty.
        Wait, looking at the results: `vpp` was $126\text{mV}$. That's actually not too bad.
        But `vavg` was $0.933\text{V}$. This means the total power delivered was very low.

    *   Let's try a different topology: **The "Buck-Boost" or "Charge Pump" approach.**
        Actually, since we have SYNC, we can use a "Synchronous" rectifier.
        If we use switches instead of diodes, we eliminate the $0.5\text{V}$ drop.
        FBR with switches:
        -   S1: pzp -> out
        -   S2: pzn -> out
        -   S3: 0 -> pzp
        -   S4: 0 -> pzn
        -   Control: G1 (edges=pos) for S1 & S3, G2 (edges=neg) for S2 & S4.
        Wait, the SYNC can only control *its* switches.
        G1 can control S1 and S3. G2 can control S2 and S4.
        This would be a fully synchronous bridge.
        $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$. With a synchronous bridge, we could potentially get $V_{out}$ up to $3.2\text{V}$.
        This would easily solve S2 and S4.
        And for S3 ($V_{oc}$ is higher there?), we can use a Zener diode to clamp the output to $3.3\text{V}$.

    *   Let's refine the Synchronous Bridge:
        -   G1: `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`. This closes when the piezo voltage $V_{pzp}$ is at its maximum.
        -   S1: `pzp` to `out`, ctrl=G1.
        -   S3: `0` to `pzp`, ctrl=G1.
        -   Wait, this is not how a bridge works.
        -   A bridge rectifier:
            -   When $V_{pzp} > V_{pzn}$: current flows `pzp` $\to$ `out` $\to$ `load` $\to$ `0` $\to$ `pzn`.
                -   Switch 1: `pzp` to `out`
                -   Switch 2: `0` to `pzn`
            -   When $V_{pzn} > V_{pzp}$: current flows `pzn` $\to$ `out` $\to$ `load` $\to$ `0` $\to$ `pzp`.
                -   Switch 3: `pzn` to `out`
                -   Switch 4: `0` to `pzp`

        -   Let's map this to our components:
            -   G1: `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`. (Controls S1 and S2)
                -   S1: `pzp` to `out`
                -   S2: `0` to `pzn`
            -   G2: `edges="neg"`, `phase=0`. (Controls S3 and S4)
                -   S3: `pzn` to `out`
                -   S4: `0` to `pzp`
